newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Restrictions on private media in new Serb law.
newsitem.headline: Restrictions on private media in new Serb law.

text.p: The Serbian government, under opposition pressure to free the state-dominated media, unveiled a press law on Monday including restrictions on privately-owned newspapers and broadcasters.
Anti-monopoly clauses in the draft said no private radio or television station would be allowed to broadcast to an audience of more then 25 percent of the 10.5 million population.
Restrictions on private press ownership said that no individual or organisation could have a holding of more than 20 percent of the total number of newspapers and magazines published in Serbia.
The limitations fell well short of demands by the Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties who are seeking to break the socialist-led government's stranglehold on Serbia's press.

Zajedno, which last month won a three- month battle to take control of Belgrade and other main towns from the socialists, have demanded that the government enter televised talks on a free press by March 20.
It threatened to boycott presidential and parliamentary elections due this year without concessions on press freedom.
Information Minister Radmila Milentijevic told a press conference she wanted a public debate on the press law which the government hopes to pass in May.
Ivan Kovacevic of the Serbian Renewal Movement (SPO), a Zajedno partner, said the draft was unacceptable and added:
"Everything that is being cooked in Mrs Milentijevic's kitchen smells of a one-party law that is going to be passed by a one-party gathering (parliament."
The draft guaranteed freedom from censorship but left the government with wide powers to stifle private media.
Publications and broadcasters will require to be licensed by an official agency and they will need to declare foreign funding or assistance.
Membership of a proposed official committee for press freedom will be heavily weighted in favour of the government.
Serbia's media is dominated by state radio and television and the daily Politika, both tightly controlled by President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist party (SPS).
